description: Join us in solving the "Harmonization of MODIS and VIIRS Hot Spots" challenge! MODIS is nearing the end of its mission, and VIIRS is taking over with higher spatial resolution—but their thermal anomaly data doesn't match out of the box. Our mission is to develop a smart calibration and harmonization model that merges both datasets into one seamless wildfire monitoring timeline.
summary:
NASA's fire record has a "jump" in it. From 2000 the MODIS sensors (on the Terra and Aqua satellites) track active fires, but in 2012 the newer VIIRS sensor arrived with much smaller pixels and started picking up far more fires. If you put the two side by side, it looks like the world suddenly started burning more, when really the instrument changed.
We built a statistical model that converts MODIS data into what VIIRS would have seen, and inversely VIIRS data into what MODIS would have seen. It learns from 2012–2024, when both were flying: 236 countries and 321 million detections. It looks at how MODIS sees each fire (how strong each detection is, how dense, from what angle), because a small crop fire and a huge forest fire need very different corrections, which is a why a simple scaling factor does not suffice.. We tested it on countries and years it never saw. Typical error dropped from 51% to 14%, and there's no jump in 2012 anymore.
The result is one continuous fire record from November 2000 to today, for anywhere on Earth. You can explore it on the Fire Globe, the webapp we deployed online: pick a country or draw an area, and switch between VIIRS and MODIS units.
We're upfront about what it can't fix. Some fires MODIS never saw at all, either because of their size or because of clouds, and orbit drift still adds a small bias after 2019, while 85% of lava and 78% of gas flares are detected as being fire-cells.
details:
NASA has tracked wildfires from space since 2000 with the MODIS sensors, but in 2012 a sharper sensor called VIIRS took over. VIIRS picks up far more fires, especially small ones, so if you put the two records side by side, fires seem to suddenly get worse in 2012. Our project fixes that: we built a model that converts the old MODIS data into what VIIRS would have seen, so you get one continuous fire record from 2000 to today. It learned from 2012 to 2024, when both sensors were flying: 236 countries and over 300 million fire detections. It also takes into account that a small crop fire and a huge forest fire need very different corrections. We tested it on countries and years it had never seen, and the error dropped from about 51% (the raw MODIS data) to 14% (our converted MODIS data). We wrote it in Python and processed everything on our own laptops and virtual machines in the cloud. The results are on the Fire Globe, a website built with JavaScript and ESRI World Imagery where you can pick any country or draw any area and see its monthly fire history since 2000. We want researchers, NGOs and anyone curious to be able to ask "are fires actually getting worse here?" and get an honest answer covering 25 years instead of 12. We're also upfront about the limits: some fires MODIS simply never saw, and satellite orbit drift adds a small bias in recent years.
Here's our presentation if you want to see more: https://eloquent-sable-681873.netlify.app/#1
